issues.legal_issue: A second appellate court must formulate a substantial question of law before reversing the findings of the courts below.
material_facts: The trial court and first appellate court found for the plaintiffs and granted mandatory injunction.
The High Court reversed those findings in second appeal without formulating a substantial question of law.
issues.conclusion: The High Court acted contrary to the requirement governing second appeals by reversing the lower courts’ findings without formulating a substantial question of law.
issues.legal_principle: Section 100(4) of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 requires the High Court to formulate the substantial question of law on which a second appeal is heard. Although the Court ordinarily might have remitted the matter, it did not do so because the dispute could be resolved in the appeal and the appellants were otherwise entitled to succeed.

predicates.second_appeal: The matter is an appeal from a decision made in second appeal.
predicates.lower_court_findings_reversed: The second appellate court reversed findings made by the courts below.
predicates.no_substantial_question_formulated: The second appellate court did not formulate a substantial question of law for its decision.

issues.definition: When a second appellate court reverses lower court findings without formulating a substantial question, that reversal is procedurally improper.

issues.legal_issue: A suit for mandatory injunction against an occupant whose licence has ended is maintainable when the licensor acts within a reasonable time, assessed in light of the circumstances.
material_facts: The property owners had permitted an occupant to construct and operate a cinema theatre under a licence, which was renewed for a further term.

The licence required the property to be returned with the structures removed at the end of the term, and the occupant died before the term ended; the lower courts found that the licence ended on his death.
The owners explained that they allowed time for the occupant’s family to wind up the business and filed suit when the agreed licence term expired.
The High Court treated the interval after the occupant’s death as unexplained delay, but did not find the owners’ explanation unacceptable.
The Supreme Court considered the explanation plausible and held that the High Court’s conclusion on delay could not stand.
issues.conclusion: The suit for mandatory injunction was maintainable in the circumstances, and the High Court’s ruling that the owners had to seek recovery of possession was set aside.
issues.legal_principle: A licensee’s occupation does not become hostile or trespassory immediately upon termination of the licence; the licensor may retain control or possession through the licensee, who may need time to wind up a business. Whether the licensor acted within a reasonable time depends on the circumstances. If the licensor fails to act promptly and the former licensee is treated as a trespasser, recovery of possession may be required. The Court applied the approach to reasonable time in Veerayee Ammal v. Seeni Ammal and the treatment of a mandatory-injunction suit as effectively one for possession in Sant Lal Jain v. Avtar Singh.

predicates.injunction_suit_after_licence_terminatio: The claimant brings an injunction suit against an occupant after the occupant’s licence has ended.
predicates.occupant_entered_with_permission: The occupant originally entered or remained on the property with the claimant’s permission.
predicates.licensor_acted_within_reasonable_time: The claimant acted within a reasonable time after termination, considering the circumstances of the case.

issues.definition: If a permitted occupant remains after the licence ends and the claimant brings an injunction suit within a reasonable time, the injunction suit is maintainable.

issues.legal_issue: Whether delay in bringing an injunction suit was unreasonable could not be decided for the first time in second appeal when the issue depended on factual assessment and had not been specifically pleaded or supported by evidence below.
material_facts: The defendants did not specifically plead before the trial court or first appellate court that the suit was barred because it had been brought after an unreasonable delay.
No evidence was led below on whether the time taken to file suit was unreasonable.
The defendants first raised the delay-based maintainability argument in the second appeal.
The owners had offered an explanation for the timing of the suit, which the Supreme Court considered plausible.
issues.conclusion: The High Court could not decide the factual dispute about reasonable time for the first time in second appeal on that record.
issues.legal_principle: The reasonableness of the time taken depends on factual circumstances and is not simply a question of law that can be raised and determined for the first time in second appeal without a factual foundation. Firm Sriniwas Ram Kumar v. Mahabir Prasad supports the principle that relief may be considered on an alternative basis where the opposing party has raised that basis and suffers no prejudice; it does not justify deciding an unpleaded factual dispute without the necessary foundation.

rule.if: second_appeal and reasonable_time_depends_on_case_facts and no_specific_delay_plea_below and no_evidence_on_delay_below

predicates.second_appeal: The challenge to the suit’s maintainability is raised in a second appeal.
predicates.reasonable_time_depends_on_case_facts: Assessing whether the claimant acted within a reasonable time requires consideration of the circumstances of the case.
predicates.no_specific_delay_plea_below: The opposing party did not specifically plead below that the claimant’s delay was unreasonable.
predicates.no_evidence_on_delay_below: No evidence was presented below to establish that the claimant’s delay was unreasonable.

issues.definition: When a delay dispute depends on the facts and was neither specifically pleaded nor supported by evidence below, it cannot be decided for the first time in second appeal.
